Andy Robertson has stressed that Liverpool’s hopes of mounting a serious push for the Premier League title under Arne Slot may depend heavily on making the team much harder to break down. The left-back pointed to the importance of defensive progress after Liverpool began the new campaign with back-to-back victories and, just as significantly, two shutouts. That start has given Slot an ideal opening as he settles into life as manager, but Robertson suggested that sterner examinations are still to come. The next one arrives at Old Trafford, where Liverpool will meet Manchester United in a fixture that should provide a much stronger measure of how solid the side really is. So far, neither Ipswich nor Brentford managed to score against Liverpool, and that has encouraged the squad after concerns over their defending last season. Robertson’s comments reflect a belief that if Liverpool can combine their usual attacking quality with greater resilience at the back, they will give themselves a much better chance of staying in the race at the top for longer than they did in the previous campaign.

handle with greater discipline at the back is, in Robertson’s view, one of the main areas in which Liverpool must improve. He noted that keeping two clean sheets from their first two league matches is exactly the kind of beginning the team would have wanted, and he made clear that the aim now is to continue that pattern. Against Manchester United, Liverpool know the challenge will be more demanding, and Robertson emphasized the need to restrict the number of opportunities their opponents are allowed to create. More broadly, he said the objective should not stop with one game; after the international break, Liverpool want to maintain that same standard against every side they face. His remarks suggest a shift in focus toward control and prevention rather than simply relying on scoring enough goals to outgun opponents. While Liverpool were still highly competitive last season, Robertson seemed to acknowledge that there were warning signs in the numbers, with the team giving away too many openings compared with their closest rivals. If that trend can be reduced, Liverpool could become far more consistent across the entire season.

Looking back on last year, Robertson effectively admitted that Liverpool’s defensive record fell short of what was required to become champions. The club let in 41 goals in 38 league games, a total notably higher than both Manchester City and Arsenal, the two teams that finished above them. City, who went on to win the title, conceded seven fewer, while Arsenal allowed 12 fewer, underlining the gap Liverpool must close if they are to overtake those sides. Robertson’s point was that even when Liverpool were still firmly involved in the title contest, they were surrendering more chances than their main competitors, and eventually that vulnerability caught up with them. In his view, when a team repeatedly gives opponents sights of goal, there will inevitably be matches in which they are punished, and that is precisely what happened as Liverpool’s challenge faded. The early evidence under Slot is encouraging, but Robertson’s message is that promise alone is not enough; Liverpool must turn those first two clean sheets into a lasting habit if they want to be genuine contenders. P.S. In essence, Robertson believes Liverpool’s route to a title challenge under their new manager will depend not just on their attacking talent, but on becoming far tougher and more dependable defensively over the long run.
